about: THE TONGUES - the words and the real lines that let speech work as Design/fate_faith_and_self.md 6c says: plain English; the period's own things by their own names; words of the speaker's tongue sprinkled in; and at a moment that matters a real line in the old tongue that turns into English piece by piece. Made 7 Oct 2026. THE RULE: nothing here is invented and passed off as old. Every word is given as a text or a dictionary has it; every line is a real line of a real text, with where it stands. HOW TO READ THE MARKS: no mark on where_attested or source means the text was read on 7 Oct 2026 (in the chest's texts_793.json, or at the page named in Design/content/lore/tongues_notes.md); (?) means it is given from knowledge of the dictionary or text and was not re-read that day, so a person who knows the tongue must check it before release. A line with check=true has an original quoted from memory. TONGUE IDS are the encounter engine's (npc_roles_793.json 'peoples'; 'latin' is used by three card lines). Cards also test tongue.norse, tongue.english and tongue.norse_more: older names for old_norse and old_english, to be folded into these. SPELLING: Old Norse words are in the normalised spelling of the dictionaries (Old West Norse, as written down in the 12th and 13th centuries); what a Dane of 800 said was a little older in sound (the stones have felaga, drængʀ, styrimannr), and the lines taken from stones keep the stones' own forms. Old English keeps each source's spelling (the chest's Beowulf has length marks and hyphens; the Exeter Book texts have none). Latin is in the spelling of the Clementine Vulgate. LINES: 'english' is the reading to credit; 'english_by' names it. Where the translator died before 1956 and the book was printed before 1931 it is free to ship. Where no free translation was found or checked, english is the game's own plain rendering and own=true (yours to edit). 'pairs' are [their words, the English for them] in order: joined with spaces, the left sides give 'original' exactly and the right sides read as English. pairs_are='translation' means the right sides joined ARE the credited english; pairs_are='plain' means they are the game's own plain word-for-word rendering, used because the credited translation moves the words about or says thee and thou (show the plain one while the line turns; keep the credited one for the chest). 'text_id' points at the same text in texts_793.json (or, where it begins 'more:', in Design/content/lore/texts_more.json). Edit freely.
about_not_before: The year before which a line should not be spoken as a living line, because the text was made then or tells of that year. A line not listed is verse, scripture, prayer or proverb older than 793 or without a date (Hávamál, Beowulf, The Wanderer, The Seafarer, the Maxims, the Durham Proverbs, the Vulgate, the Mass, the Rule, the baptismal vow, the Weissenburg prayer, the Breastplate) and may be used in any life. In the first life (793-805) the dated lines that fit are those of 793 to 798.

tongues.name: Norse (the Danish tongue)
tongues.written_then: runes on stone, wood and metal; the verse and sagas were written down from the 12th century on
tongues.note: One tongue from Jutland to the Lofoten in 793; its own speakers later called it the Danish tongue (dönsk tunga) whoever spoke it. A Northman and an Englishman could trade and quarrel each in his own speech, slowly, with the endings lost: a workable half-understanding. The kin numbers in this file are the game's judgment, not a measurement.

tongues.name: English
tongues.written_then: yes: laws, charters, verse, glosses; the Chronicle from the 890s
tongues.note: Four dialects in 793 (Northumbrian, Mercian, Kentish, West Saxon); most of what survives is later West Saxon. Frisian is its nearest kin, and the English missionaries of the 8th century went to the Frisians and the Old Saxons because they could preach to them without an interpreter (Bede, Ecclesiastical History V.9-10) (?). They called their speech Englisc and themselves Angelcynn.

tongues.name: Latin (the tongue of the Church)
tongues.written_then: yes: nearly everything that was written in the West
tongues.note: Nobody's mother tongue by 793 and every churchman's second one: the one speech that works from Armagh to Aachen. It is learned, not inherited (the engine's 'learn latin'), so kinship does not help with it. A clerk half follows the Romance of Gaul; in 813 the council of Tours ordered sermons put 'into the rustic Roman tongue or the German' because the people no longer followed Latin (?). The psalms a Frankish monk sang were Jerome's Gallican psalter, which is the Vulgate's; an English monk of 793 still sang the older Roman psalter, close to it.

tongues.name: Saxon
tongues.written_then: a little: the baptismal vow (8th century), the Heliand and Genesis (c. 830-850), a few blessings and lists
tongues.note: The tongue of the Saxons between Rhine and Elbe, who were being conquered and baptised by Charles from 772 to 804: in the first life (793-805) it is a tongue under the sword. The Heliand tells the Gospel as the story of a lord and his men, with ships, storms and sea words: the best store of period sea-speech on the Continent. Scholars dispute whether the baptismal vow is Saxon, Low Frankish (Old Dutch) or coloured by English; it may have been used at Utrecht.

tongues.name: Frankish (of the Rhine)
tongues.written_then: the Low Frankish behind Dorestad: almost nothing. The Rhine Frankish of Mainz and Worms: yes, from c. 800 (catechism, oaths, the Ludwigslied)
tongues.note: What the Franks of the lower Rhine and Meuse spoke in 793 was never written down as connected speech. So the words and lines here are Old High German in its Rhine Frankish form (the Weissenburg catechism of c. 800, the Strasbourg oaths of 842, the Ludwigslied of 881-2), which a Frank of Cologne or Mainz spoke and a Frank of Dorestad would follow; each entry says where it is from. The Franks called it theodisca lingua, 'the tongue of the people' (Royal Frankish Annals 788) (?), the word that became both Deutsch and Dutch. Frankish lords in Neustria also spoke Romance: that is learning, not kinship.

tongues.name: Frisian
tongues.written_then: no. About two dozen short rune inscriptions (5th to 10th century); the first connected Frisian is a psalm gloss of c. 1100 and the law books of 1276-1300
tongues.note: THE HARD CASE, and the player's own people at Dorestad. Nothing a Frisian of 793 said was written down. The words given here are the oldest attested forms, from the law books of the 13th century (whose law is partly older), each marked as such. No whole line of Frisian turns, because none exists from the period: a Frisian speaks English with these words sprinkled in, and for a verse or an oath the game may use the nearest kin, Old English or Old Saxon, and must say so in the credits. The name Kapman is itself Frisian: kapmon, the merchant (?).

tongues.name: Irish
tongues.written_then: yes, richly: glosses, verse, law, annals (from the 7th century)
tongues.note: No kin among the other tongues of the game: to a Frank or a Northman it is closed until learned. Its bridge to everyone is the Latin of its monks. The annals of the first life are written half in Latin and half in Irish, and their word for the raiders is geinti, 'heathens'.

tongues.name: Wendish (West Slavic)
tongues.written_then: no. Names in Frankish and Saxon Latin; the Slavic written nearest in time is Old Church Slavonic (from 863), a southern kin
tongues.note: VERY LITTLE CAN BE GIVEN. The Obodrites and Wilzi of the Baltic shore left no writing, and their speech died out by the 18th century. What is honest: names as the Latin writers heard them (marked 'in Latin sources') and a few trade words in Old Church Slavonic (marked 'kin'), which a Wend would have said in nearly the same shape. No line turns.

tongues.name: Romance (the rustic Roman tongue)
tongues.written_then: one text: the oath of Strasbourg, 842; then the Sequence of St Eulalia, c. 880
tongues.note: What the townsfolk of Quentovic, Rouen and Paris spoke: no longer Latin, not yet French. The only connected piece from the first century of the game is the oath Louis the German swore at Strasbourg so that the army of his brother would understand him.

tongues.name: Baltic (Prussian, Curonian)
tongues.written_then: no. Old Prussian is first written c. 1400 (?)
tongues.note: Nothing attested from the period but names in Wulfstan's report (Truso, Witland, the Estas). No words are given and no line turns: the Balts speak through an interpreter, in English.

tongues.name: Finnic
tongues.written_then: no. A birch-bark letter from Novgorod (13th century) is the oldest (?)
tongues.note: Nothing attested from the period. The one sure trace is in other tongues: Ruotsi, the Finnic name for the Swedes, is the likeliest root of the name Rus (?). No words are given.

words.means: whole, well, in luck: the greeting, to a man (heil to a woman, heilir to several)
words.where_attested: Hávamál 2 'Gefendr heilir!'; Vafþrúðnismál 4 'Heill þú farir!' (Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no)
words.use: Heill, steersman. Where are you out of?

words.where_attested: Vafþrúðnismál 4, Frigg to Odin as he sets out
words.use: The wind is yours by noon. Heill þú farir.

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary (1874), s.v. vel-kominn (?)
words.use: Velkominn. There is ale, and room by the fire.

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. þökk (?)
words.use: Þökk for the bread. I will not forget it.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 110 'Baugeið Óðinn' (a ring-oath)
words.use: I will not take your word. I will take your eiðr, on the ring.

words.means: a ring: the arm-ring of silver that is also money, and the ring that oaths are sworn on
words.where_attested: Hávamál 110 'Baugeið' (ring-oath)
words.use: He broke a piece off his baugr and laid it on my scale.

words.means: a bargain made fast by a clasp of hands before witnesses
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. hand-sal (?)
words.use: No need of more words. Handsal, here, with these two watching.

words.means: truce: safety given to a man for a time or in a place
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. grið (?); the English borrowed it: The Battle of Maldon, 'grið fæstnian' (in the chest)
words.use: You have grið in this harbour till the market ends. After that, look to yourself.

words.means: a man without honour: the worst name there is, and a matter for the law
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. níðingr (?); the English borrowed it: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1049 'for niðing' (?)
words.use: A man who leaves his partner on a lee shore is a níðingr, and I will say so at the thing.

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. tröll (?); Njáls saga ch. 36 (?)
words.use: Three pennies for that hide? Troll hafi þik.

words.where_attested: the great Jelling stone (DR 42, c. 965): 'faþur sin', his father
words.use: My faðir sailed this coast before there was a toll on it.

words.where_attested: the great Jelling stone (DR 42): 'muþur sina', his mother
words.use: The cloth is my móðir's weaving. Feel it.

words.where_attested: the Glavendrup stone (DR 209, early 10th century): 'Alla syniʀ', Alli's sons
words.use: This is my sonr. He rows, and he keeps his mouth shut.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 89 'Bróðurbana sínum' (his brother's killer)
words.use: My bróðir has the other half of the ship.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 76 'deyja frændr'
words.use: Go to Ribe and ask for my frændi. He will stand surety for you.

words.means: partner: one who has laid his goods together with yours (fé-lag) for a voyage
words.where_attested: the Hedeby stone of Erik (DR 1, c. 995): 'Erik, felaga sin'; Hávamál 52 'fekk ek mér félaga'
words.use: Ask my félagi. Half of what is in this hull is his.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 43 'Vin sínum skal maðr vinr vera'
words.use: A vinr of mine at Birka will give you a fair weight.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 2 'Gestr er inn kominn'
words.use: You are a gestr here. Sit, eat, and then say what you want.

words.where_attested: the Mervalla stone (Sö 198, 11th century): 'Svæin, sinn bonda'
words.use: The bóndi owns the landing. You pay him, not the king.

words.where_attested: the Glavendrup stone (DR 209): 'hans kona'
words.use: My kona keeps the keys and the scales when I am at sea.

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. kaup-maðr (?); Egils saga ch. 50 (?)
words.use: I am a kaupmaðr, not a raider. Look in the hull.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 52 'oft kaupir sér í litlu lof'; 83 'magran mar kaupa' (buy a horse lean)
words.use: Will you kaupa, or only handle the goods?

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. kaupangr (?); the place Kaupang in Vestfold, Ohthere's 'Sciringes heal'
words.use: There is a kaupangr two days north. They pay well for wine.

words.means: an ounce of silver, an eighth of a mark (plural aurar)
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. eyrir (?); the Forsa ring (Hs 7): 'aura' (?)
words.use: One eyrir for the knife, or six aurar for the lot, weighed on your scales or mine.

words.means: a mark: eight ounces of silver by weight
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. mörk (?)
words.use: The ship cost me twelve mörk of silver and a winter of work.

words.means: cattle; wealth; money (one word for all three)
words.where_attested: Hávamál 76 'Deyr fé'
words.use: He has the fé to buy your whole cargo and not feel it.

words.means: a gift (which asks a gift back)
words.where_attested: Hávamál 42 'ok gjalda gjöf við gjöf' (and pay gift with gift)
words.use: Take it as a gjöf. You will know what to bring me next year.

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. skattr (?)
words.use: The Finns pay their skattr in furs, and the furs come to me.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 74 'skips ráar' (the yards of a ship); 82 'á skip skal skriðar orka'
words.use: Whose skip is that, drawn up past the tide line?

words.means: the broad, deep trading ship that goes on the open sea
words.where_attested: the Mervalla stone (Sö 198): 'dyrum knærri', in a costly knörr
words.use: A knörr will carry it. A longship would have to leave half on the beach.

words.means: longship: the narrow ship of war
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. lang-skip (?); in English as 'langscipu', Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 896 (?)
words.use: Two langskip in the sound, and neither has cargo aboard.

words.means: steersman: the master of a ship
words.where_attested: the Hedeby stone of Erik (DR 1): 'han was styrimannr'
words.use: I speak for this ship. I am her stýrimaðr.

words.means: a young man of good stuff; a good fellow
words.where_attested: the Hedeby stone of Erik (DR 1): 'drængʀ harþa goþr', a very good drengr
words.use: Take the boy. He is a drengr, and he does not get sick.

words.where_attested: the Mervalla stone (Sö 198): 'Hann oft siglt til Sæimgala'
words.use: We sigla at first light if the wind holds.

words.means: the yard that carries the sail
words.where_attested: Hávamál 74 'skammar ro skips ráar' (short are the yards of a ship)
words.use: Lower the rá. I will not carry sail into that.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 82 'veðri á sjó róa' (in fair weather row out to sea)
words.use: No wind. We róa, and you take an oar like the rest.

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. stjórn-borði (?)
words.use: Keep the skerry on the stjórnborði and you will clear it.

words.means: the stem: the prow of a ship
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. stafn (?)
words.use: Put a man in the stafn with a pole. The channel shifts.

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. akkeri (?)
words.use: Drop the akkeri here and wait for the flood.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 82 'á sjó'
words.use: The sjór is quiet today. It will not be tomorrow.

words.means: a wind to sail by: a fair wind
words.where_attested: Hávamál 90 'í byr óðum' (in a raging wind)
words.use: Give me three days of byrr and I am in Kaupang.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 82 'veðri á sjó róa'; 88 'veðr ræðr akri' (weather rules the field)
words.use: Veðr rules the sea as it rules the field. We wait.

words.means: half a day and night: twelve hours. Distances at sea are told in dœgr of sailing
words.where_attested: Landnámabók: 'sjau dœgra sigling' from Stad in Norway to Horn in Iceland (in the chest, text 'landnama')
words.use: It is four dœgr with a good wind, and nobody can tell you more than that.

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. vík (?)
words.use: Lie up in the vík tonight. There is fresh water at its head.

words.means: a sea-raider. A trade, not a people: a man goes 'í víking', raiding, and comes home a farmer
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. víkingr (?); the Härlingstorp stone (Vg 61): 'í víkingu' (?)
words.use: He was a víkingr for two summers. Now he sells what he took.

words.means: the chief who keeps the holy place and leads the offerings
words.where_attested: the Glavendrup stone (DR 209): 'goþa wea', goði of the holy places
words.use: Speak to the goði before you cut wood in that grove.

words.where_attested: the Glavendrup stone (DR 209): 'wea'
words.use: No weapon is drawn in the vé. Leave yours at the gate.

words.where_attested: the Glavendrup stone (DR 209): 'þur uiki þasi runaʀ', Thor hallow these runes
words.use: New keel, new mast. Þórr vígi.

words.means: to make an offering to the gods
words.where_attested: Hávamál 144 'Veistu, hvé blóta skal?' (do you know how to offer?)
words.use: They blóta at midwinter, and no stranger sails before it is done.

words.means: the first sign of the cross: taken by heathen traders so that they could deal and eat with Christians, without baptism
words.where_attested: Egils saga ch. 50 (?); Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. prím-signa (?)
words.use: I took the prímsigning at Dorestad. It costs nothing and it opens doors.

words.means: the assembly of free men, where law is spoken and suits are settled
words.where_attested: Hávamál 61 'ríði maðr þingi at'; 25 'er at þingi kemr'
words.use: Bring it to the þing. I will not settle it on a beach.

words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. lög (?)
words.use: That is lög here: a wreck belongs to the man who owns the shore.

words.means: an outlaw: a man put outside the law, whom anyone may kill
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. útlagi (?)
words.use: Do not carry him. He is útlagi from here to the Sound.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 81 'öl, er drukkit er' (praise ale when it is drunk)
words.use: Öl first. Then we talk about your price.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 19 'drekki þó at hófi mjöð' (drink mead, but in measure)
words.use: The mjöðr is for the feast. You get ale.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 52 'með halfum hleif' (with half a loaf)
words.use: Half a hleifr and a place at the oar: that is the bargain.

words.means: food for the road: the stores of a voyage
words.where_attested: Hávamál 74 'sá er nesti trúir' (he who trusts his stores)
words.use: We have nest for nine days. Do not make it ten.

words.where_attested: the great Jelling stone (DR 42): 'Haraldr kunungʀ'
words.use: The konungr takes his share at Hedeby, and his men count well.

words.means: earl: a great man under a king, or over a land that has none
words.where_attested: Cleasby-Vigfusson s.v. jarl (?)
words.use: The jarl holds the fjord. Nothing passes without a gift to him.

words.where_attested: the Glavendrup stone (DR 209): 'æft drottin sin', after his lord
words.use: I carry this for my dróttinn, and it is not for sale.

words.means: a free man of standing; the sworn man of a lord
words.where_attested: the Glavendrup stone (DR 209): 'heþwærþan þægn', an honoured þegn
words.use: He is a þegn, and his word at the thing is worth three of mine.

words.means: a following: a ship's company, a war band
words.where_attested: the Glavendrup stone (DR 209): 'liþs' (of the lið)
words.use: He came with a lið of forty. That is not a trading crew.

words.where_attested: Hávamál 87 'sjalfráða þræli' (a slave who has his own way)
words.use: The þræll goes with the farm. I am not selling him apart.

words.means: be well: the greeting (wesað hāle to several). It is the root of 'wassail'
words.where_attested: Beowulf 407 'Wæs þū, Hrōðgār, hāl!' (?)
words.use: Wes hāl, shipman. You are early this year.

words.means: a welcome one: a guest gladly seen
words.where_attested: Maxims I 94 'leof wilcuma Frysan wife' (Exeter Book)
words.use: You are a wilcuma in this house, and so is your silver.

words.means: dear one: the polite word to a lord, an elder or a stranger of standing, where we say 'sir'
words.where_attested: Maxims I 94 'leof'; as an address, the Fonthill Letter, 'Leof, ic ðe cyðe' (?)
words.use: Lēof, I ask only that the toll be taken on what I sell, not on what I carry.

words.means: safe and sound: the wish at parting
words.where_attested: Beowulf 318 'sīða gesunde' (safe on your ways), the blessing of the coast watchman
words.use: Go gesund, and God keep the wind behind you.

words.where_attested: Beowulf 1778 'Þæs sig metode þanc' (thanks be to God for that)
words.use: Gode þanc, you are come. We thought the ship lost.

words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller, An Anglo-Saxon Dictionary, s.v. āð (?); laws of Alfred 1 (?)
words.use: My āð is good in this shire. Ask the reeve how many will swear with me.

words.means: a pledge: the thing or the promise given to bind a bargain
words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller s.v. wedd (?); laws of Alfred 1 'his að and his wed' (?)
words.use: Leave the ring as wedd, and take the wool now.

words.where_attested: Maxims II 32 'Treow sceal on eorle' (Cotton Tiberius B.i)
words.use: I dealt with your father on his trēow alone. Shall I with you?

words.means: truce, protection for a time (a Norse word the English took up)
words.where_attested: The Battle of Maldon: 'wē willað wið þām golde grið fæstnian' (in the chest)
words.use: The king's grið covers the market. It does not cover the road home.

words.means: peace: the settled peace between peoples or within a land
words.where_attested: The Battle of Maldon: 'and niman frið æt ūs' (in the chest); Durham Proverbs 24 'Forworht mann friþes behofað'
words.use: There is frið with the Danes this summer, and their ships come to trade.

words.means: woe: the cry of grief or of cursing (wā lā wā, alas)
words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller s.v. wā (?)
words.use: Wā to the man who sold me this rope.

words.where_attested: Durham Proverbs 22 'Earh mæg þæt an þæt he him ondræde' (a coward can do one thing only: be afraid)
words.use: Call me a hard dealer if you like. Do not call me earh.

words.where_attested: Durham Proverbs 11 'cwæþ sē þe geseah hægtessan'
words.use: Some hægtesse has looked at this butter. It will not come.

words.where_attested: Beowulf 316 'fæder alwalda'; The Wanderer 115 'Fæder on heofonum'
words.use: My fæder had this berth before me, and paid the same toll.

words.means: kinsman (plural māgas); the kindred that pays and takes the price of a man
words.where_attested: The Wanderer 109 'hēr bið mǣg lǣne'; Durham Proverbs 13 'Gemǣne sceal māga feoh' (the goods of kinsmen are shared)
words.use: He is my mǣg. If you cheat him you have cheated nine of us.

words.where_attested: The Wanderer 108 'hēr bið frēond lǣne'; Durham Proverbs 2 'Frēond dēah feor ge nēah'
words.use: I have a frēond at Quentovic who will house you.

words.means: friend; a lord who is a friend
words.where_attested: Maxims I 144 'Wel mon sceal wine healdan on wega gehwylcum'
words.use: Hold on to a wine on every road, the saying goes. I hold on to you.

words.means: a free farmer; a husband; plainly, a man
words.where_attested: Maxims I 96 'hyre ceorl to ham' (her husband home); Durham Proverbs 10 'cwæð se ceorl'
words.use: He is a ceorl with a boat, no more. But his oath stands in court.

words.where_attested: Maxims I 95 'Frysan wife'; 100 'Wif sceal wiþ wer wære gehealdan'
words.use: Ask my wīf. She keeps the tally while I am at sea.

words.where_attested: laws of Alfred 34 'Eac is ciepemonnum gereht' (?); laws of Ine 25 (?)
words.use: I am a cīepemann out of Dorestad, and the reeve knows my face.

words.where_attested: Geþyncðo 6 'gif massere geþeah' (if a merchant throve) (?)
words.use: A massere who crosses the sea three times in his own ship may sit with the thanes. So they say.

words.where_attested: Ælfric, Colloquy: 'ond cype mine þingc' (and sell my things), in the chest
words.use: I cȳpan cloth here and buy tin. Nothing else.

words.where_attested: Ælfric, Colloquy: 'ond bicge dyrwyrþe þingc' (and buy precious things), in the chest
words.use: If you will not bicgan before witnesses, you will not buy from me.

words.means: a load: the cargo of a ship
words.where_attested: Ælfric, Colloquy: 'mid hlæstum minum' (with my cargo), in the chest
words.use: The hlæst is wool and hides. Open any bale you like.

words.means: cattle; goods; money (one word for all three)
words.where_attested: The Wanderer 108 'hēr bið feoh lǣne'; The Battle of Maldon: 'feoh wið frēode' (in the chest)
words.use: He wants feoh in the hand, not a promise for Michaelmas.

words.means: a coin; money; in Kent a twentieth of a shilling
words.where_attested: The Battle of Maldon: 'mid þām sceattum' (in the chest)
words.use: Count the sceattas twice. Some of them are clipped.

words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller s.v. pening (?)
words.use: Four pening the fleece, and I am robbing myself.

words.means: tribute; rent; what is paid to be left in peace
words.where_attested: The Battle of Maldon: 'mid gafole forgyldon', 'tō gafole gāras syllan' (in the chest)
words.use: The town paid gafol to the ships, and the ships are still in the river.

words.means: the toll on goods bought and sold
words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller s.v. toll (?)
words.use: The toll is the tenth penny, and the reeve takes it before you leave the strand.

words.means: a town with a market and a harbour
words.where_attested: Ohthere's report (Old English Orosius): 'án port on suðeweardum þæm lande, þone man hæt Sciringes heal', in the chest
words.use: There is no port north of here, only farms. Buy your water now.

words.means: a trading place by the water (Lundenwic, Hamwic, Gipeswic, Eoforwic)
words.where_attested: laws of Hlothhere and Eadric 16 'in Lundenwic' (?)
words.use: The wīc lies outside the old walls, along the strand.

words.means: reeve: the officer of the king who witnesses sales and takes the toll
words.where_attested: laws of Alfred 34 'beforan kyninges gerefan' (?); Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787 'se gerefa' (?)
words.use: Show the gerēfa every man you take inland. He will count them.

words.where_attested: Wulfstan's report: 'þæt scip wæs ealne weg yrnende under segle' (in the chest); Maxims I 93 'Scip sceal genægled'
words.use: The scip is sound. It is the crew I doubt.

words.where_attested: Beowulf 238 'brontne cēol'; Maxims I 96 'biþ his ceol cumen'; Maxims II 24 'Mæst sceal on ceole'
words.use: A Frisian cēol came up on the flood this morning.

words.means: a ship ('floater'); a seaman; in the plural, raiders in ships
words.where_attested: Beowulf 218 'flota fāmig-heals'; Maxims I 95 'þonne flota stondeð'; The Battle of Maldon: 'þā flotan stōdon gearowe' (in the chest)
words.use: Three flotan off the ness, and none of them showing a shield. Traders, I think.

words.where_attested: Wulfstan's report: 'yrnende under segle' (running under sail), in the chest
words.use: Under segl all the way, seven days and nights.

words.where_attested: Maxims II 24 'Mæst sceal on ceole'
words.use: She lost her mæst off the sands and came in under oars.

words.where_attested: Beowulf 303 'on ancre fæst' (fast at anchor)
words.use: Lie to your ancor till the ebb. The bar will kill you now.

words.means: the steering side: the right side of a ship
words.where_attested: Ohthere's report: 'þæt weste land on ðæt steorbord' (in the chest)
words.use: Keep the land on the stēorbord for three days and you cannot miss it.

words.means: the left side of a ship: the side at the back of the steersman
words.where_attested: Ohthere's report: 'þa widsæ on ðæt bæcbord' (in the chest)
words.use: Open sea on the bæcbord, and nothing in it but whales.

words.where_attested: Maxims I 103 'Lida biþ longe on siþe'; The Battle of Maldon: 'sǣlida', 'lidmen' (in the chest)
words.use: A lida is long away. His wife knows it when she weds him.

words.means: a pirate, a sea-raider (never the name of a people)
words.where_attested: The Battle of Maldon: 'wīcinga ār' (the messenger of the raiders), 'wīcinga fela' (in the chest)
words.use: Wīcingas took two boats off the Swale last week. Sail in company.

words.where_attested: Beowulf 318 'ic tō sǣ wille'; The Wanderer 4 'hrīmcealde sǣ'
words.use: Over sǣ they pay twice what we do for English cloaks.

words.where_attested: Maxims II 23 'Stream sceal on yðum'; The Seafarer 35 'sealtyþa gelac' (the play of the salt waves)
words.use: The ȳða are short and steep on that bar. Take it at the top of the flood.

words.means: the flood tide; the sea in flood (the ebb is ebba)
words.where_attested: The Battle of Maldon: 'sē flōd ūt gewāt' (the flood went out), in the chest
words.use: Wait for the flōd. Nothing with a keel crosses before it.

words.where_attested: Ohthere's report: 'ælce dæge hæfde ambyrne wind' (in the chest)
words.use: With an ambyre wind it is a month under sail. Without one, do not ask.

words.where_attested: The Wanderer 5 'wyrd bið ful ārǣd'; Beowulf 455, 572; Maxims II 5 'wyrd byð swiðost'
words.use: We did what men can do. The rest is wyrd.

words.means: the Lord (once any lord of a war band; by 793 it means God)
words.where_attested: Beowulf 1779 'ēcean drihtne' (the eternal Lord)
words.use: Drihten keep us off that shore tonight.

words.means: heathen: one who is not baptised
words.where_attested: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 793 'heðenra manna hergung' (the raiding of heathen men), in the chest
words.use: He is hǣðen, but he has never given me short weight.

words.means: a minster: a church with its community of monks or priests
words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller s.v. mynster (?)
words.use: The mynster buys wine, wax and oil, and pays in good pennies.

words.means: man-price: what the life of a man is worth in law, paid to his kin if he is killed
words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller s.v. wer-gild (?); laws of Ine and Alfred (?)
words.use: Kill a thane's man and you owe his wergild. You do not have it.

words.means: a judgment; a law laid down; the good name a man leaves
words.where_attested: Durham Proverbs 10 'on swīnes dōme'; Beowulf 1388 'dōmes ǣr dēaðe'; The Battle of Maldon: 'on hyra sylfra dōm' (in the chest)
words.use: I will take the reeve's dōm on it, and so will you.

words.means: the folk-moot: the public meeting where a reeve hears suits and witnesses dealings
words.where_attested: laws of Alfred 34 'on folcgemote' (?)
words.use: Say it at the folcgemōt, before the reeve, or do not say it.

words.means: witness: the men who saw the bargain made
words.where_attested: laws of Ine 25 'beforan gewitnessum' (?)
words.use: No sale without gewitnes. If the goods prove stolen, they are what saves you.

words.where_attested: Durham Proverbs 8 'Hwīlum æfter medo menn mǣst geþyrsteð'
words.use: Medu tonight, and thirst in the morning, as the saying has it.

words.means: a loaf: bread. A lord is a hlāford, a loaf-keeper
words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller s.v. hlāf (?)
words.use: A hlāf and a cheese for each man, and no more till we raise land.

words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller s.v. ealu (?)
words.use: The ealu here is thin. Bring your own if you stay the week.

words.where_attested: Maxims II 1 'Cyning sceal rice healdan'
words.use: The cyning has forbidden the sale of horses over sea.

words.means: the chief man of the king over a shire
words.where_attested: The Battle of Maldon: 'wīs ealdorman' (in the chest)
words.use: The ealdorman is at the ford with the levy. Trade can wait.

words.means: a thane: a man who serves the king or a lord and holds land for it
words.where_attested: The Battle of Maldon: 'þegenas' (in the chest)
words.use: He is a þegn of the king, so mind how you weigh for him.

words.means: a man of high birth; a brave man (after Cnut, an earl)
words.where_attested: Beowulf 573 'unfǣgne eorl'; Maxims II 32 'Treow sceal on eorle'
words.use: An eorl keeps his word or he is no eorl.

words.means: lord: the loaf-keeper who feeds and protects his men
words.where_attested: Bosworth-Toller s.v. hlāford (?); 'hlafordleas' (lordless) stands in an Exeter riddle in the chest
words.use: My hlāford sent me with this, and he will want an answer.

words.means: thanks be to God; also what the porter of a monastery answers when a stranger knocks
words.where_attested: Rule of Benedict 66: the porter answers 'Deo gratias' or 'Benedic'
words.use: Deo gratias, the ship is in. Now, where is the wine?

words.means: 'bless me': how a monk greets one who comes to the gate
words.where_attested: Rule of Benedict 66
words.use: Benedic. You have come far, by your boots. Come in to the guest house.

words.where_attested: Ruth 2:4 (Vulgate): 'Dominus vobiscum'; the greeting of the priest at Mass
words.use: Dominus vobiscum, shipmen. Is there one among you who can carry a letter to Utrecht?

words.where_attested: John 20:19 (Vulgate) (?)
words.use: Pax vobis. Put up your knives: this is the feast of Saint Martin.

words.where_attested: Ruth 2:4 (Vulgate): the reapers' answer
words.use: You have dealt fairly with this house. Benedicat tibi Dominus.

words.where_attested: Mark 5:34; Luke 7:50 (Vulgate) (?)
words.use: The abbot has your tithe of wax. Vade in pace.

words.means: Lord, have mercy (Greek, kept whole in the Latin service)
words.where_attested: Rule of Benedict 9 and 17 (?); the Mass
words.use: When the mast went, the priest sang Kyrie eleison and the Danes rowed. Both helped.

words.where_attested: Psalm 50:3 (Vulgate) 'Miserere mei, Deus' (?)
words.use: Miserere, he said, and gave the beggar his own cloak.

words.means: if the Lord wills: what a Christian adds to any plan
words.where_attested: James 4:15 (Vulgate), spoken to merchants who plan a year of trade
words.use: I will be back at Michaelmas with the wine, si Dominus voluerit.

words.means: an oath, sworn on relics or the Gospel book
words.where_attested: Nithard, Histories III.5, of the oaths at Strasbourg (?); the Romance of the oath itself has 'sagrament'
words.use: A count's word is not a sacramentum. Make him swear it on the bones.

words.means: cut off from the Church and accursed
words.where_attested: 1 Corinthians 16:22; Galatians 1:8 (Vulgate) (?)
words.use: Whoever robs this altar, anathema sit: let him be cut off.

words.where_attested: Deuteronomy 27:17 (Vulgate) 'Maledictus qui transfert terminos proximi sui' (?)
words.use: Maledictus, says the Law, is the man who moves his neighbour's boundary stone.

words.where_attested: Proverbs 11:1 (Vulgate): 'Statera dolosa abominatio est apud Dominum'
words.use: A false weight is an abominatio, merchant, and I have seen yours.

words.means: the Lord (God). For a living lord, an abbot or a king, clerks wrote the short form domnus
words.where_attested: Psalm 106:24 'opera Domini'; Rule of Benedict 63: the abbot is to be called 'dominus et abbas'
words.use: Dominus sent the wind, and the steersman did the rest.

words.means: abbot: the father of a house of monks
words.where_attested: Rule of Benedict 63; Annals of Ulster (CELT), entries of the 790s: 'abbatis'
words.use: Nothing leaves the cellar without a word from the abbas.

words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster (CELT): 'episcopus Rechrainne'
words.use: The episcopus has the king's ear, and a tenth of the toll.

words.means: brother: how an older monk names a younger, and one Christian another
words.where_attested: Rule of Benedict 63: 'fratrum nomine'
words.use: Frater, the guest is cold. Bring the fire to him, not him to the fire.

words.means: 'reverend father': how a younger monk must address an elder
words.where_attested: Rule of Benedict 63: 'iuniores autem priores suos nonnos vocent'
words.use: Ask nonnus Gerwald. He kept the gate when the last Frisian fleet came up.

words.means: the whole community of a monastery: monks, servants and tenants
words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster 806.8: 'Familia Iae occisa est a gentilibus'
words.use: The familia of this house is two hundred mouths. We buy grain by the shipload.

words.where_attested: Rule of Benedict 53: 'Omnes supervenientes hospites tamquam Christus suscipiantur'; Matthew 25:35 'hospes eram'
words.use: You are a hospes, so you eat before we ask your business.

words.means: a stranger far from home; a pilgrim
words.where_attested: Rule of Benedict 53: 'domesticis fidei et peregrinis'
words.use: He is a peregrinus bound for Rome. Carry him to Quentovic for the love of God, or for a penny.

words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster 794.7: 'a gentilibus'; 802.9: 'a gentibus'
words.use: A gentilis may buy here. He may not stay the night inside the wall.

words.where_attested: Alcuin to King Æthelred, 793: 'a pagana gente' (in the chest, quoted there from memory) (?)
words.use: Paganus or not, his silver is pure. Weigh it and see.

words.where_attested: Matthew 13:45 (Vulgate): 'homini negotiatori, quaerenti bonas margaritas'
words.use: The kingdom of heaven is like a negotiator, the Gospel says. Do not look so pleased.

words.means: a huckster: one who sells by the small measure
words.where_attested: Ecclesiasticus 26:28 (Vulgate): 'non justificabitur caupo a peccatis labiorum'
words.use: Scripture says a caupo is hardly clean of the sins of his lips. Name your price again.

words.where_attested: Proverbs 11:1 (Vulgate): 'Statera dolosa'
words.use: Bring the statera of the minster. I trust it more than yours.

words.where_attested: Proverbs 11:1 (Vulgate): 'pondus aequum voluntas ejus' (a just weight is his will)
words.use: One pondus and one measure in all the realm: so the king has ordered.

words.where_attested: Matthew 20:2 (Vulgate) (?); capitulary of Frankfurt, 794, c. 5 (?)
words.use: Twelve loaves of wheat for one denarius. That is the law since Frankfurt.

words.means: a shilling: twelve pennies. A sum to reckon in, not a coin in the hand
words.where_attested: the Frankish laws and capitularies, throughout (?)
words.use: The fine is one solidus a head. Count it out: twelve pennies each.

words.where_attested: Matthew 9:9 (Vulgate) 'sedentem in telonio' (?); the Frankish toll charters (Design/content/lore/law_tolls.md 3.1)
words.use: The teloneum at Dorestad is the tenth part, and no bishop's letter frees you of it.

words.means: a slave, as a thing bought and sold
words.where_attested: capitulary of Herstal, 779, on the sale of mancipia (?) (Design/content/lore/law_tolls.md 14)
words.use: No mancipium is sold beyond the march, and none in secret.

words.where_attested: Psalm 106:23 (Vulgate): 'Qui descendunt mare in navibus'
words.use: Each navis that lies at this bank pays the bank its penny.

words.means: a haven; a landing and trading place
words.where_attested: Psalm 106:30 (Vulgate): 'in portum voluntatis eorum'
words.use: He brought them to the portus they wished for. Pray it is so with you.

words.where_attested: Psalm 92:4 'elationes maris'; Psalm 76:20 'In mari via tua' (Vulgate)
words.use: The mare gives and the mare takes. Tithe what it gives.

words.where_attested: Psalm 106:25 'spiritus procellae'; 106:29 'statuit procellam ejus in auram' (Vulgate)
words.use: He turned the procella into a breeze once. Ask him again.

words.where_attested: Psalm 68:16 (Vulgate): 'Non me demergat tempestas aquae'
words.use: No ship left in that tempestas, thank God, so none was lost.

words.where_attested: Matthew 8:27 (Vulgate): 'venti et mare obediunt ei'
words.use: The ventus obeys one master, and he is not your steersman.

words.where_attested: Psalm 106:24 'mirabilia ejus in profundo'; Psalm 68:16 (Vulgate)
words.use: What goes into the profundum stays there till the last day.

words.where_attested: Mark 8:36 (Vulgate): 'detrimentum animae suae'; Psalm 68:2
words.use: What does it profit you to gain the whole cargo and lose your anima?

words.where_attested: Ecclesiasticus 26:28 (Vulgate): 'a peccatis labiorum' (from the sins of the lips)
words.use: Short measure is a peccatum before it is a crime.

words.where_attested: the dismissal of the Mass, 'Ite, missa est' (?)
words.use: No market before the missa is sung. Then sell what you like.

words.where_attested: the Lord's Prayer: 'Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie'
words.use: Panis and beans today. It is a fast day, and you are in a minster.

words.where_attested: Psalm 103:15 (Vulgate) 'vinum laetificet cor hominis' (?)
words.use: The vinum is for the altar first. What is left, we may sell you.

words.where_attested: Heliand 259: 'Hêl uuis thu, Maria' (text of the Bibliotheca Augustana)
words.use: Hêl uuis thu, Frisian. What do you bring up the river?

words.where_attested: Heliand 259: 'thu bist thînun hêrron liof' (you are dear to your lord)
words.use: My hêrro holds this bank of the river, and the toll with it.

words.means: lord of a following; the Lord
words.where_attested: Heliand 2279: 'drohtines craftu' (by the power of the Lord)
words.use: A man without a drohtin is a man anyone may rob.

words.where_attested: Heliand 1600: 'Fadar ûsa'; the baptismal vow: 'got alamehtigan fadaer'
words.use: My fadar swore to the old gods, and I to the new. We both kept the market.

words.where_attested: Heliand 265: 'môdar mid mannun'
words.use: The amber was my môdar's. I will not sell it for cloth.

words.where_attested: the baptismal vow: 'in crist godes suno'
words.use: This is my suno. He will bring the salt next year, not I.

words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 14: 'bêđea thea gebrôđar' (both the brothers), of Andrew and Peter
words.use: We are gebrôđar, and one answers for the other.

words.means: friendship (friund is friend and kinsman both)
words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 4: 'hald incan friundskepi uuel' (keep your friendship well)
words.use: There has been friundskepi between our houses since my grandfather. Do not end it over a cask.

words.where_attested: the baptismal vow: 'the hira genotas sint' (who are their companions)
words.use: He is my genôt on this road. Ask him if I lie.

words.means: a companion: a man of the following of a lord (plural gesîđos)
words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 14: 'samnode gesîđos' (he gathered companions)
words.use: He rides with six gesîđos. Do not haggle long.

words.means: the sworn man of a lord
words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 4: 'ên thegan'
words.use: I am the count's thegan, and I speak with his mouth.

words.means: a man; a man of birth
words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 14: 'erlo gemang' (among men)
words.use: No erl of this land sells his horse to a stranger.

words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 14: 'cuninges iungoron' (the follower of a king)
words.use: We had no cuning before the Franks came. We had the meeting at Marklo.

words.where_attested: Heliand 1195: 'treuua habda he gôda' (he had good faith), of Matthew the toll man
words.use: Give me your treuua on it, and your hand.

words.means: I forsake: the first words of the vow a Saxon said at the font
words.where_attested: the Old Saxon baptismal vow (Vatican, Pal. lat. 577): 'ec forsacho diabolae'
words.use: I said ec forsacho with the water on my head and a Frankish spear at my back.

words.where_attested: Heliand 2254: 'gilôƀo is iu te luttil' (your faith is too small); the baptismal vow: 'ec gelobo'
words.use: His gilôƀo is new, and he wears it like a new shoe.

words.means: an offering to devils: the churchmen's word for heathen sacrifice
words.where_attested: the Old Saxon baptismal vow: 'end allum diobolgelde'
words.use: The priest calls it diobolgeld. My mother called it feeding the well.

words.means: Thunaer and Woden and Saxnot: the three gods a Saxon had to name and forsake
words.where_attested: the Old Saxon baptismal vow
words.use: They made me say it aloud: Thunaer ende Uoden ende Saxnote. I have not said the names since.

words.where_attested: the Old Saxon baptismal vow: 'allum them unholdum'
words.use: Some unhold sits in that ford. Three carts this year.

words.means: tribute and toll: what Matthew took for his lord
words.where_attested: Heliand 1195: 'tins endi tolna'
words.use: Tins endi tolna, to the count, at every bridge. It was not so before.

words.means: protection: the hand a lord holds over his people
words.where_attested: Heliand 2233: 'sô mahtiges mundburd' (the protection of one so mighty)
words.use: A trader in this land buys the mundburd of some lord first, and cloth second.

words.where_attested: Heliand 2282: 'gaf im uuiđ thie fîund friđu' (gave him peace against the fiends)
words.use: There is friđu on the market field, by old custom.

words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 14: 'an ênero côpstedi', where Matthew sits at the toll
words.use: Bardowick is the côpstedi the Franks allow us. Go no further east with swords to sell.

words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 14: 'gold endi siluƀar'
words.use: Siluƀar by weight. I do not know your king's face on a penny.

words.means: a treasure, a costly thing (plural mêđmos)
words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 14: 'diurie mêđmos' (dear treasures)
words.use: That sword is a mêđom. It is given, not sold.

words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 14: 'geƀa managa' (many a gift)
words.use: First the geƀa to the lord of the hall. Then you may open your bales.

words.means: a nailed ship: planks made fast with iron
words.where_attested: Heliand fitt 14: 'nettiu endi neglitskipu' (nets and nailed ships)
words.use: A neglitskip like yours would feed my smith for a year in rivets.

words.means: a horned ship: high at stem and stern
words.where_attested: Heliand 2266: 'hôh hurnidskip'
words.use: A hôh hurnidskip came up the Weser, and every child ran to the bank.

words.where_attested: Heliand 2237: 'an ênna nacon innan'; 2265: 'the naco furđor skreid'
words.use: Take the naco across. The ford is too high for a cart.

words.where_attested: Heliand 2238: 'Segel up dâdun'
words.use: Up with the segel. The wind is behind us at last.

words.where_attested: Heliand 2239: 'uuederuuîsa uueros' (weather-wise men)
words.use: Hire a man who is uuederuuîs before you hire one who is strong.

words.means: the sea; a great water (also meri)
words.where_attested: Heliand 2243: 'thie sêu uuarđ an hruoru' (the sea was in uproar); 2245 'thiu meri'
words.use: I have never seen the sêu. The river is enough water for me.

words.where_attested: Heliand 2242: 'ûđiun uuahsan' (the waves grew)
words.use: The ûđia come over the low side when she is loaded so.

words.where_attested: Heliand 2242: 'ûst up stîgan' (a gale rose)
words.use: When the ûst comes down the river, tie up and wait.

words.where_attested: Heliand 2241: 'thes uuedares craft' (the might of the storm)
words.use: No man bargains with uuedar.

words.means: whole, well: the greeting (heil wis thu, be well)
words.where_attested: Old High German Tatian 3,2 'Heil wis thu' (East Frankish, c. 830) (?)
words.use: Heil, Frisian. The count wants a word before you unload.

words.where_attested: the Strasbourg oaths (842, Rhine Frankish): 'In Godes minna'
words.use: Got knows I paid the toll. Ask him, or ask the toll man.

words.means: love: 'in godes minna', for the love of God, opens an oath or a toast
words.where_attested: the Strasbourg oaths (842): 'In Godes minna ind in thes christianes folches'
words.use: In godes minna, drink. Then tell me what the Danes are paying for swords.

words.where_attested: the Strasbourg oaths (842), the oath of the army: 'Oba Karl then eid ... geleistit'
words.use: He swore an eid to the king, and another to me. I know which he will keep.

words.where_attested: the Strasbourg oaths (842): 'soso man mit rehtu sinan bruodher scal'
words.use: By what reht do you live, stranger? Frankish, Frisian or Saxon?

words.means: a matter, a dealing; an assembly
words.where_attested: the Strasbourg oaths (842): 'in nohheiniu thing ne gegango' (I will enter into no dealing)
words.use: I will have no thing with a man who sells Frankish mail to Wends.

words.where_attested: the Strasbourg oaths (842): 'tesan minan bruodher'
words.use: My bruodher keeps the vineyard. I keep the boat.

words.where_attested: the Weissenburg catechism (c. 800, South Rhine Frankish): 'Fater unsēr'
words.use: My fater shipped wine to Dorestad when the old king lived.

words.means: son and father together: one word for the pair
words.where_attested: Hildebrandslied line 4 (Fulda, c. 830)
words.use: They came aboard sunufatarungo, the old man and the boy, with one cloak between them.

words.where_attested: the Strasbourg oaths (842), the oath of the army: 'Ludhuuuig min herro'
words.use: My herro the count takes the tenth. What is left is between you and me.

words.where_attested: Ludwigslied line 4 (881-2, Rhine Frankish): 'Holoda inan truhtin'
words.use: Truhtin has kept the river open this winter. Thank him and sail.

words.where_attested: Ludwigslied line 1 (881-2): 'Einan kuning uueiz ih'
words.use: The kuning is at Nijmegen, and every boat on the Waal is carrying for him.

words.where_attested: the Weissenburg catechism (c. 800): 'quaeme rīchi thīn'
words.use: One weight and one penny in all the rīchi. That is the order.

words.where_attested: the Strasbourg oaths (842): 'thes christianes folches'
words.use: The folc of this town remember who sold them rotten grain.

words.where_attested: Hildebrandslied line 3 (c. 830): 'untar heriun tuem' (between two armies)
words.use: The heri goes against the Saxons at midsummer, and it wants bread.

words.where_attested: Ludwigslied line 2: 'Ther gerno gode thionot' (who gladly serves God)
words.use: I thionōn the bishop, and the bishop pays late.

words.where_attested: Ludwigslied line 2: 'Ih uueiz her imos lonot' (I know he will repay him)
words.use: Carry it safe and the abbot will lōnōn you well.

words.means: a debt; guilt (one word for both)
words.where_attested: the Weissenburg catechism (c. 800): 'farlāz uns sculdhi unsero' (forgive us our debts)
words.use: There is a sculd between us from last autumn. Pay it before you buy.

words.where_attested: the Weissenburg catechism (c. 800): 'scolōm unserēm' (our debtors)
words.use: He is my scolo for two casks, and he knows it.

words.where_attested: the Paris Conversations 51-58 (a phrase book for Romance speakers, 10th or 11th century): 'Gimer min ros'
words.use: Gimer the weights. I will set them on the scale myself.

words.where_attested: the Paris Conversations 51: 'Gimer min ros' (da mihi meum equum)
words.use: A ros for the towpath costs more than the oarsmen it saves.

words.where_attested: the Paris Conversations 57: 'Gimer min matzer' (cultellum)
words.use: A good matzer with a horn handle: two pennies, and it will outlast you.

words.where_attested: the Paris Conversations 58: 'Gimer cherize' (candela)
words.use: Wax for the cherize of every altar from here to Mainz comes up this river.

words.where_attested: the Weissenburg catechism (c. 800): 'Brooth unseraz emezzīgaz gib uns hiutu'
words.use: Brooth, cheese and thin wine. That is the fare of a boatman.

words.where_attested: the Weissenburg catechism (c. 800): 'ni gileidi unsih in costunga'
words.use: A chest of silver left open is a costunga for any man.

words.where_attested: the Weissenburg catechism (c. 800): 'arlōsi unsih fona ubile' (deliver us from evil)
words.use: Ubil take the man who cut my mooring.

words.means: 'the foreigners': the Romance speakers of Gaul and Italy (the same word as Welsh)
words.where_attested: the Kassel glosses (Bavarian, c. 810): 'Tole sint uualha, spahe sint peigira'
words.use: The uualha at Quentovic talk fast and weigh slow.

words.where_attested: Ludwigslied line 24 (881-2): 'Heigun sa Northman harto biduuungan' (?)
words.use: The Northman came up the Scheldt again. Hide the wine.

words.where_attested: Old High German glosses for Latin mercator (?)
words.use: I am a koufman of Mainz, under the king's protection, with his letter.

words.where_attested: Old High German Tatian (c. 830): 'in skef' (?)
words.use: A skef that draws so little can go as far as Worms.

words.where_attested: Ludwigslied line 11: 'obar seo lidan' (to come over the sea) (?)
words.use: They come over the sēo each spring, like the storks.

words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language (dil.ie) s.v. fo-chen (?)
words.use: Fo chen, stranger. Is it wine you carry, or news?

words.means: a blessing (from Latin benedictio), given at meeting and at parting
words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. bennacht (?)
words.use: Bennacht on your ship and on all who row her.

words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. buide (?)
words.use: Buide to you for the salt. The brothers had none since Lent.

words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. lugae (?)
words.use: A king's lugae outweighs yours, merchant. Bring men to swear with you.

words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. mallacht (?)
words.use: Mallacht on the hands that broke the shrine.

words.where_attested: the Breastplate of St Patrick (Stokes, The Tripartite Life, 1888): 'Crist lim. Crist remam.'
words.use: Críst between us and that sail.

words.means: heathens: the first name the annals give the Northmen
words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster 795.3: 'Loscadh Rechrainne o geinntib'
words.use: The geinti were at Rechru. Nothing is left there to buy or to sell.

words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster (CELT), of Blathmac on Iona: 'Martre Blaimhicc m. Flainn o genntib'
words.use: He would not say where the shrine was hidden, and so he had his martrae.

words.means: a shrine: the box that holds the bones of a saint
words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster 798.2: 'scrin Do Chonna do briseadh'
words.use: They carried the scrín inland in a cart, under hay.

words.where_attested: Pangur Bán (Reichenau Primer, 9th century): 'oc mu lebran'
words.use: I have my lebrán and my cat. What would I do with silver?

words.means: going into exile for the love of God: pilgrimage
words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. ailithre (?)
words.use: I am on ailithre, and I will take any ship that goes away from home.

words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster (CELT), 9th-century entries: 'Orgain Glinne Da Locha o genntib'
words.use: There was an orgain at the island. Sell your wine somewhere that still has a roof.

words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster 798.2: 'borime na crich do breith' (the cattle-tribute of the lands was taken)
words.use: The king takes his bórime in cows. He has no use for your pennies.

words.means: a cow: the measure of all wealth in Ireland
words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. bó (?)
words.use: Three bó for the cask, and that is the last word.

words.means: a bondwoman; also a sum of value, reckoned at three cows
words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. cumal (?); the law tract Críth Gablach (?)
words.use: The honour of a bishop is priced at seven cumal. Mind how you speak to him.

words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. cennaige (?)
words.use: A cennaige from the Franks comes each summer with wine for the altar.

words.means: a fair: the great gathering of a people, with games, law and trade
words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. óenach (?)
words.use: Come to the óenach at Lammas. Every king in the province will be there to buy.

words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster (CELT), 9th century: 'co ructha i l-longa' (they were carried off into ships)
words.use: A long of the heathens holds sixty men. Count the sails and do the sum.

words.means: a boat of hides on a frame of wicker
words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. curach (?)
words.use: Three of us in a curach, and nothing between us and the sea but an oxhide.

words.where_attested: the Breastplate of St Patrick: 'fudomna mara' (the depth of the sea); Annals of Ulster 798.2 'innreda mara' (raids by sea)
words.use: The muir was our wall. It is their road now.

words.where_attested: the quatrain in the St Gall Priscian (c. 850): 'fairggae findfholt' (in the chest)
words.use: When the fairrge is white, the monks sleep sound.

words.where_attested: the quatrain in the St Gall Priscian: 'Is acher in gáith in nocht'; the Breastplate: 'luathi gaithi'
words.use: A hard gáeth from the west, thank God. No ship will come from the north in it.

words.where_attested: the Breastplate of St Patrick: 'ar bádudh' (against drowning)
words.use: Say the prayer against bádud before you take that boat out.

words.means: king (there are many: of a people, of a province, of Tara)
words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster (CELT), 9th century: 'Mael Brighti a r-ri' (Máel Brigte their king)
words.use: Which rí? There are five between here and the river.

words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. tigerna (?)
words.use: The tigerna of this shore takes the first cask of any ship that lands.

words.means: foreigners: once the Gauls, then the Northmen
words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster (CELT), 9th century: 'organ Gall' (a raid on, or of, the foreigners)
words.use: The Gaill have a camp at the black pool, and they trade from it like honest men.

words.means: the land the Northmen come from
words.where_attested: the quatrain in the St Gall Priscian: 'dond láechraid lainn úa Lothlind'
words.use: You have been to Lothlind? Then tell me why they come.

words.where_attested: the quatrain in the St Gall Priscian: 'dond láechraid lainn' (the fierce warriors)
words.use: A láechrad landed at dusk. By morning the church had no bell.

words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster (CELT), 9th century: 'Canannan a brathair' (Canannán his brother)
words.use: My bráthair is abbot there. Say my name at the gate.

words.means: son (every man is named 'mac' of his father)
words.where_attested: Annals of Ulster, throughout, written short as 'm.': 'Blaimhicc m. Flainn'
words.use: I am Colmán mac Ailella, and my father was known in this port.

words.where_attested: Dictionary of the Irish Language s.v. cuirm (?)
words.use: Cuirm for the crew, and wine for the steersman, if he will talk.

words.means: merchant: the name of the game
words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century and later; Hofmann and Popkema, Altfriesisches Handwörterbuch (2008) s.v. kāpmon (?)
words.use: I am a kāpmon of Dorestad, and my father was one before me.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century; Hofmann and Popkema s.v. kāp (?)
words.use: A kāp made before two neighbours stands. One made in the dark does not.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century; Hofmann and Popkema s.v. panning (?)
words.use: Not a panning less. The cloak is Frisian, and you know what that means.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century: 'skipu' (Bremmer, An Introduction to Old Frisian, 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: Four skipu went down the Lek this morning, all for England.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: A Frisian is free tō farane up the Rhine and down it. King Charles said so.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century; Hofmann and Popkema s.v. sē (?)
words.use: The sē took my grandfather's land. I trade because I have none to plough.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century; Hofmann and Popkema s.v. dīk (?)
words.use: Every man mends his length of the dīk, or loses his land.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: Mind the fiskdam below the bend. You will pay for every stake you break.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: The liōde chose the law here, not a count.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century, in the Weser dialect (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: The kining of the Franks takes the toll now. Before him it was Redbad.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: Charles is keiser now, they say. The toll is the same.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: Speak to the hāvedmon of the boatmen. He sets the pilot's price.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: From here to the Weser is one rīke now, and one toll after another.

words.means: the officer who summons men to court and sees the judgment done
words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century: 'skelta', glossed in Latin as iudex (Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: The skelta will call you by name three times. Be there the first.

words.means: the law-sayer: the man who speaks the law in court
words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century: 'aesgha', glossed in Latin as iudex (Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: Ask the āsega what a broken oar is worth. He has the whole law in his head.

words.where_attested: the Old Frisian law books: 'Freeska Landriucht' (Frisian land law), the name of the printed collection of c. 1485
words.use: That is Frisian riucht. A Frank may not judge me by his.

words.means: life; and the price of a life: wergild
words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century: 'lyf', wergild (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: He owes a whole līf to that kindred, and he is paying it in cloth.

words.means: freedom: 'a free neck', with no collar on it
words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century; Hofmann and Popkema s.v. frīhals (?)
words.use: A Frisian keeps his frīhals as long as he keeps his dike.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century; Hofmann and Popkema s.v. ēth (?)
words.use: Twelve hands on the ēth, and the debt is cleared.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: Keep to the herestrēte. Off it, a stranger who does not shout is taken for a thief.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century: 'Godi', to God (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: God and Saint Willibrord keep this boat. And I keep the bailer.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: The godeshūs at Utrecht owns a tenth of this river, on parchment.

words.means: a blessing: the sign of the cross (from Latin signum)
words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: Take the priest's seininge before you cross the bar. It weighs nothing.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: He was my partner. He is my fīand since the night he sold my share.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: The diōvel made that sandbank and moves it every winter.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century: 'wiif' (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: My wīf will know the ship by her sail before I see the roof.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century (Bremmer 2009, as cited in Wikipedia, 'Old Frisian')
words.use: My swāger has the next berth. Between us we hold the whole bank.

words.where_attested: Old Frisian law books, 13th century; Hofmann and Popkema s.v. feder (?)
words.use: My feder taught me the sands. Nobody taught me the Franks.

words.means: a comb: one of the few Frisian words written down in the period itself, in runes
words.where_attested: rune inscriptions on combs from Oostum and Toornwerd, Groningen, 8th to 9th century (Looijenga, Texts and Contexts of the Oldest Runic Inscriptions, 2003) (?)
words.use: A kabu of antler, cut at Dorestad. The Danes buy them by the sack.

words.means: the name the Wilzi gave themselves
words.where_attested: in Latin sources: Einhard, Life of Charles 12, 'Wilzi, qui propria lingua Welatabi dicuntur' (?)
words.use: The Franks call them Wilzi. They call themselves Welatabi, and they do not like Franks.

words.means: the Obodrites: the Wends of the western Baltic shore, allies of Charles
words.where_attested: in Latin sources: Royal Frankish Annals 789, 798, 808 (?)
words.use: The Abodriti hold the coast from Kiel fjord to the Warnow, and the market at Reric.

words.means: the trading place of the Obodrites, which the Danish king emptied in 808
words.where_attested: in Latin sources: Royal Frankish Annals 808 (?)
words.use: Reric paid the Danish king a great toll. So he took its merchants home with him.

words.means: 'the old fort': the stronghold of the Wagrians, which the Saxons called Aldinburg
words.where_attested: in Latin sources: Helmold, Chronicle of the Slavs I.12 (12th century) (?)
words.use: Their prince sits at Starigard. Bring him salt, and a gift for his gods.

words.means: Svarozhits: the god of the Redarians at Riedegost
words.where_attested: in Latin sources: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicle VI.23 (c. 1015) (?)
words.use: They cast lots before Zuarasici for every war and every long voyage.

words.means: Svantevit: the god of Arkona on Rügen, to whom merchants paid a share
words.where_attested: in Latin sources: Helmold, Chronicle of the Slavs I.52 and II.12 (12th century) (?)
words.use: No stranger trades at Arkona without a gift to Zuantevith first.

words.means: prince (kin: Old Church Slavonic; borrowed from Germanic kuning)
words.where_attested: kin: Old Church Slavonic, 10th- and 11th-century manuscripts (?)
words.use: The kъnędzь takes a tenth of every cargo, and he counts himself.

words.means: merchant (kin: Old Church Slavonic; the root is borrowed from Germanic kaup)
words.where_attested: kin: Old Church Slavonic, 10th- and 11th-century manuscripts (?)
words.use: A kupьcь is safe among them while the market peace holds.

words.means: a market (kin: Old Church Slavonic; the Northmen borrowed it as torg)
words.where_attested: kin: Old Church Slavonic, 10th- and 11th-century manuscripts (?)
words.use: The trъgъ is on the open ground by the bridge, every eighth day.

words.means: a guest; a merchant from abroad (kin: Old Church Slavonic)
words.where_attested: kin: Old Church Slavonic, 10th- and 11th-century manuscripts (?)
words.use: You are a gostь here. Eat the bread and the salt, and then we deal.

words.where_attested: kin: Old Church Slavonic, 10th- and 11th-century manuscripts (?)
words.use: Sьrebro by weight, or linen cloths by the count. Not pennies.

words.where_attested: kin: Old Church Slavonic, 10th- and 11th-century manuscripts (?)
words.use: They go up the river in a ladii cut from one tree.

words.where_attested: kin: Old Church Slavonic, 10th- and 11th-century manuscripts (?)
words.use: Medъ and wax are what they sell, and slaves, and they sell them cheap.

words.means: the sea (kin: Old Church Slavonic). Pomerania is po morje: 'by the sea'
words.where_attested: kin: Old Church Slavonic, 10th- and 11th-century manuscripts (?)
words.use: The people by the morje know amber. The people inland know only what it fetches.

words.means: 'the mute ones': the Slavs' name for the Germans, who cannot speak properly (kin: Old Church Slavonic)
words.where_attested: kin: Old Church Slavonic and later; in Greek dress in the 10th century (?)
words.use: To them we are all Němьci: men who make noises instead of words.

words.where_attested: the oath of Strasbourg (842): 'Pro Deo amur', 'in quant Deus sauir et podir me dunat'
words.use: Deus gave me a boat and a bad back. I thank him for the boat.

words.means: love: 'pro Deo amur', for the love of God
words.where_attested: the oath of Strasbourg (842): 'Pro Deo amur et pro christian poblo'
words.use: Pro Deo amur, lend me a rope. Mine went with the tide.

words.where_attested: the oath of Strasbourg (842), the oath of the army: 'Si Lodhuvigs sagrament ... conservat'
words.use: He gave his sagrament on the altar of Saint Josse. I was there.

words.where_attested: the oath of Strasbourg (842): 'cist meon fradre Karlo'
words.use: My fradre is toll man at the bridge. You will pay less if you say my name.

words.where_attested: the oath of Strasbourg (842), the oath of the army: 'Karlus meos sendra'
words.use: My sendra the abbot owns the salt pans, and the men who work them.

words.where_attested: the oath of Strasbourg (842): 'pro christian poblo'
words.use: The poblo of this town speak as I do. The count speaks Frankish at home.

words.where_attested: the oath of Strasbourg (842): 'si cum om per dreit son fradra saluar dist'
words.use: Per dreit the wreck is the count's. In truth it is whoever gets there first.

words.means: a pact, a plea, a sitting of the court (from Latin placitum)
words.where_attested: the oath of Strasbourg (842): 'nul plaid nunquam prindrai'
words.use: The count holds his plaid after Easter. Bring your witnesses then.

words.where_attested: the oath of Strasbourg (842): 'in adiudha et in cadhuna cosa'; the oath of the army: 'in nulla aiudha'
words.use: I owe him aiudha in a fight, by my oath. I do not owe him my cargo.

lines.original: Deyr fé, deyja frændr, deyr sjalfr it sama, en orðstírr deyr aldregi, hveim er sér góðan getr.
lines.english: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, And so one dies one's self; But a noble name will never die, If good renown one gets.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (New York, 1923)
pairs: And so one dies one's self;
lines.source: Hávamál 76 (Codex Regius, c. 1270; the verse is older). Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: any Northman of standing; an old steersman over a dead shipmate
lines.when_it_fits: a death aboard; a burial; when the player's good name is at stake

lines.original: Deyr fé, deyja frændr, deyr sjalfr it sama, ek veit einn, at aldrei deyr: dómr um dauðan hvern.
lines.english: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, And so one dies one's self; One thing now that never dies, The fame of a dead man's deeds.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: And so one dies one's self;
The fame of a dead man's deeds.
lines.source: Hávamál 77. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no. (dómr is 'judgment': what is said of each of the dead)
lines.who_would_say_it: a Northman; the narrator's voice on the last day
lines.when_it_fits: the last day of a life, when the house is reckoned up

lines.original: Ungr var ek forðum, fór ek einn saman, þá varð ek villr vega; auðigr þóttumk, er ek annan fann, maðr er manns gaman.
lines.english: Young was I once, and wandered alone, And nought of the road I knew; Rich did I feel when a comrade I found, For man is man's delight.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: And nought of the road I knew;
lines.source: Hávamál 47. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: a Northman who takes the player as partner or friend
lines.when_it_fits: a first bond; the making of a félag; meeting a known face in a far port

lines.original: Gefendr heilir! Gestr er inn kominn, hvar skal sitja sjá?
lines.english: Hail to the giver! a guest has come; Where shall the stranger sit?
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
lines.source: Hávamál 2. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: the player's Norse host, or the player entering a Norse hall
lines.when_it_fits: the first time the player is a guest in the North

lines.original: Elds er þörf, þeims inn er kominn ok á kné kalinn; matar ok váða er manni þörf, þeim er hefr um fjall farit.
lines.english: Fire he needs who with frozen knees Has come from the cold without; Food and clothes must the farer have, The man from the mountains come.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: þeim er hefr um fjall farit.
who has come over the fell.
lines.source: Hávamál 3. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: a Norse host, a farmer's wife, a goði
lines.when_it_fits: coming ashore after a hard crossing; winter quarters

lines.original: Vits er þörf, þeim er víða ratar; dælt er heima hvat;
lines.english: Wits must he have who wanders wide, But all is easy at home;
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: But all is easy at home;
lines.source: Hávamál 5, first half. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: an old Norse trader to a young one
lines.when_it_fits: the first voyage beyond the home waters; after the player is cheated

lines.original: Byrði betri berr-at maðr brautu at en sé mannvit mikit; auði betra þykkir þat í ókunnum stað;
lines.english: A better burden may no man bear For wanderings wide than wisdom; It is better than wealth on unknown ways,
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
lines.source: Hávamál 10, lines 1-5. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: a Norse steersman; a father sending a son to sea
lines.when_it_fits: setting out with an empty hull and a plan; a Lore test passed

lines.original: Afhvarf mikit er til ills vinar, þótt á brautu búi, en til góðs vinar liggja gagnvegir, þótt hann sé firr farinn.
lines.english: Crooked and far is the road to a foe, Though his house on the highway be; But wide and straight is the way to a friend, Though far away he fare.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: is the road to a foe,
Though his house on the highway be;
en til góðs vinar liggja gagnvegir,
But wide and straight is the way to a friend,
lines.source: Hávamál 34. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: a Norse friend met again after years
lines.when_it_fits: a long voyage made to see one person; a bond renewed

lines.original: Ganga skal, skal-a gestr vera ey í einum stað; ljúfr verðr leiðr, ef lengi sitr annars fletjum á.
lines.english: Forth shall one go, nor stay as a guest In a single spot forever; Love becomes loathing if long one sits By the hearth in another's home.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: By the hearth in another's home.
lines.source: Hávamál 35. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: a Norse host, not unkindly
lines.when_it_fits: the player has wintered too long in one port; the welcome wears thin

lines.original: Bú er betra, þótt lítit sé, halr er heima hverr;
lines.english: Better a house, though a hut it be, A man is master at home;
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: A man is master at home;
lines.source: Hávamál 36, first half. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: a Norse farmer; a crewman who wants to go home
lines.when_it_fits: the house at home is in question; a crewman asks to be paid off

lines.original: Vápnum sínum skal-a maðr velli á feti ganga framar, því at óvíst er at vita, nær verðr á vegum úti geirs of þörf guma.
lines.english: Away from his arms in the open field A man should fare not a foot; For never he knows when the need for a spear Shall arise on the distant road.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: skal-a maðr velli á feti ganga framar,
in the open field A man should fare not a foot;
því at óvíst er at vita,
nær verðr á vegum úti geirs of þörf guma.
when the need for a spear Shall arise on the distant road.
lines.source: Hávamál 38. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: a Norse crewman; a hired sword
lines.when_it_fits: going ashore in a strange place; a strange sail closing

lines.original: Vin sínum skal maðr vinr vera, þeim ok þess vin;
lines.english: To his friend a man a friend shall prove, To him and the friend of his friend;
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: a man a friend shall prove,
To him and the friend of his friend;
lines.source: Hávamál 43, first half. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: a Northman vouching for the player, or asking the player to vouch
lines.when_it_fits: an introduction; a favour asked through a friend

lines.original: með halfum hleif ok með höllu keri fekk ek mér félaga.
lines.english: With half a loaf and a half-filled cup A friend full fast I made.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: A friend full fast I made.
lines.source: Hávamál 52, second half. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no; English: sacred-texts.com/neu/poe/poe04.htm. (The word is félagi: a partner)
lines.who_would_say_it: a Northman remembering how a partnership began
lines.when_it_fits: the player shares food with a stranger; a félag is made

lines.original: Ár skal rísa, sá er annars vill fé eða fjör hafa; sjaldan liggjandi ulfr lær of getr né sofandi maðr sigr.
lines.english: He must early go forth who fain the blood Or the goods of another would get; The wolf that lies idle shall win little meat, Or the sleeping man success.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: sá er annars vill fé eða fjör hafa;
who fain the blood Or the goods of another would get;
lines.source: Hávamál 58. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no; English: sacred-texts.com/neu/poe/poe04.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: a raider; a hard trader
lines.when_it_fits: a rival sails before dawn; a raider explains himself

lines.original: Nótt verðr feginn sá er nesti trúir, skammar ro skips ráar; hverf er haustgríma; fjölð of viðrir á fimm dögum en meira á mánuði.
lines.english: He welcomes the night whose fare is enough, (Short are the yards of a ship,) Uneasy are autumn nights; Full oft does the weather change in a week, And more in a month's time.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: (Short are the yards of a ship,)
fjölð of viðrir á fimm dögum
Full oft does the weather change in a week,
And more in a month's time.
lines.source: Hávamál 74. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no; English: sacred-texts.com/neu/poe/poe04.htm. (fimm dögum is 'five days': the old northern week)
lines.who_would_say_it: a Norse steersman reading the sky
lines.when_it_fits: an autumn crossing; choosing whether to sail or wait

lines.original: At kveldi skal dag leyfa, konu, er brennd er, mæki, er reyndr er, mey, er gefin er, ís, er yfir kemr, öl, er drukkit er.
lines.english: Give praise to the day at evening, to a woman on her pyre, To a weapon which is tried, to a maid at wedlock, To ice when it is crossed, to ale that is drunk.
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: Give praise to the day at evening,
to a woman on her pyre,
To a weapon which is tried,
To ice when it is crossed,
lines.source: Hávamál 81. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no
lines.who_would_say_it: any Northman, drily
lines.when_it_fits: the player counts a gain before the ship is home

lines.original: Í vindi skal við höggva, veðri á sjó róa,
lines.english: When the gale blows hew wood, in fair winds seek the water;
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
pairs: When the gale blows hew wood,
