in fair winds seek the water;
lines.source: Hávamál 82, lines 1-2. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no; English: sacred-texts.com/neu/poe/poe04.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: a Norse steersman or pilot
lines.when_it_fits: wind-bound in harbour; the choice to wait for weather

lines.original: Heill þú farir! heill þú aftr komir! heill þú á sinnum sér!
lines.english: Safe mayst thou go, safe come again, And safe be the way thou wendest!
lines.english_by: Henry Adams Bellows (d. 1939), The Poetic Edda (1923)
lines.source: Vafþrúðnismál 4: Frigg to Odin as he sets out. Old Norse: Guðni Jónsson's text, heimskringla.no; English: sacred-texts.com/neu/poe/poe05.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: a Norse wife, mother or friend on the shore
lines.when_it_fits: the player leaves a Norse port where someone cares whether he comes back

lines.original: Þor wigi þæssi runaʀ.
lines.english: May Thor hallow these runes.
lines.source: the Glavendrup stone, Funen (DR 209), early 10th century; carved 'þur uiki þasi runaʀ'. Reading as in the Rundata text given by Wikipedia, 'Glavendrup stone'
lines.who_would_say_it: a rune carver; a goði; a Dane at a grave
lines.when_it_fits: a stone is raised for a dead Dane; the player has runes cut (from c. 900; for the first life use the word Þórr vígi only)

lines.original: Þorulfʀ resþi sten þænsi, hemþægi Swens, æftiʀ Erik, felaga sin, æs warþ døþr, þa drængiaʀ satu um Heþaby; æn han was styrimannr, drængʀ harþa goþr.
lines.english: Thorulf raised this stone, the house-man of Svein, after Erik, his partner, who met his death when the fighting men sat round Hedeby; and he was a steersman, a very good man.
pairs: when the fighting men sat round Hedeby;
lines.source: the stone of Erik at Hedeby (DR 1), c. 995. Reading as in the Rundata text given by Wikipedia, 'Stone of Eric'
lines.who_would_say_it: nobody: it is read from the stone at Hedeby
lines.when_it_fits: a later life (after 995) at Hedeby; a model for the stone a partner raises for the player

lines.original: Sigrið let ræisa stæin þenna at Svæin, sinn bonda. Hann oft siglt til Sæimgala, dyrum knærri, um Domisnæs.
lines.english: Sigrid had this stone raised for Svein, her husband. He often sailed to Semgallen, in a costly knörr, round Domesnes.
lines.source: the Mervalla stone, Södermanland (Sö 198), 11th century. Reading as in the Rundata text given by Wikipedia, 'Baltic area runestones'. The second sentence is verse
lines.who_would_say_it: a widow; the stone itself
lines.when_it_fits: a later life in the Baltic; the stone the player's own widow might raise

lines.original: Haraldr kunungʀ baþ gørwa kumbl þøsi æft Gorm, faþur sin, ok æft Þorwi, moþur sina, sa Haraldr æs seʀ wan Danmork alla ok Norwæg ok dani gærþi kristna.
lines.english: King Harald had this monument made after Gorm, his father, and after Thyra, his mother: that Harald who won for himself all Denmark, and Norway, and made the Danes Christian.
pairs: that Harald who won for himself
lines.source: the great Jelling stone (DR 42), c. 965. Reading as in the Rundata text given by Wikipedia, 'Jelling stones'
lines.who_would_say_it: nobody: it is read from the stone at Jelling
lines.when_it_fits: a later life (after 965): the hour when the Danes turn

lines.original: Wyrd oft nereð unfǣgne eorl, ðonne his ellen dēah!
lines.english: Weird often saveth The undoomed hero if doughty his valor!
lines.english_by: John Lesslie Hall (d. 1928), Beowulf: An Anglo-Saxon Epic Poem (Boston, 1892)
pairs: a man not yet marked to die,
lines.source: Beowulf 572-573 (MS c. 1000; the poem is older)
lines.who_would_say_it: an English thane or shipman; the player's own crew
lines.when_it_fits: after a storm or a fight the ship should not have lived through

lines.original: Gǣð ā Wyrd swā hīo scel!
lines.english: Goes Weird as she must go!
lines.source: Beowulf 455
lines.who_would_say_it: any Englishman facing a risk he has chosen
lines.when_it_fits: before a Nerve test with death on it; the moment of casting off into bad weather

lines.original: Hwæt syndon gē searo-hæbbendra byrnum werede, þē þus brontne cēol ofer lagu-strǣte lǣdan cwōmon, hider ofer holmas helmas bǣron?
lines.english: Who are ye men here, mail-covered warriors Clad in your corslets, come thus a-driving A high riding ship o'er the shoals of the waters, And hither 'neath helmets have hied o'er the ocean?
pairs: who come with so tall a ship
lines.source: Beowulf 237-240, the coast watchman's challenge (the last half-line is the reading of Harrison and Sharp's edition, as in the chest)
lines.who_would_say_it: an English reeve or coast watchman riding down to a strange ship
lines.when_it_fits: the first landing on an English shore; the Portland landing of 789 told as it should have gone

lines.original: Gewāt þā ofer wǣg-holm winde gefȳsed flota fāmig-heals fugle gelīcost
lines.english: The foamy-necked floater fanned by the breeze, Likest a bird, glided the waters
pairs: Then over the waves she went,
the ship with foam at her neck,
lines.source: Beowulf 217-218
lines.who_would_say_it: an English poet in hall; a crewman who knows the verse
lines.when_it_fits: the first fair wind in a new ship; the ship window, once

lines.original: Ǣghwæðres sceal scearp scyld-wiga gescād witan, worda and worca, sē þe wēl þenceð.
lines.english: The difference surely 'Twixt words and works, the warlike shield-bearer Who judgeth wisely well shall determine.
lines.source: Beowulf 287-289, the coast watchman's answer
lines.who_would_say_it: a reeve or watchman who has heard the player's fair story
lines.when_it_fits: after a Tongue test: he lets the player pass and will remember what he does

lines.original: Mǣl is mē tō fēran; fæder alwalda mid ār-stafum ēowic gehealde sīða gesunde! ic tō sǣ wille, wið wrāð werod wearde healdan.
lines.english: 'Tis time I were faring; Father Almighty Grant you His grace, and give you to journey Safe on your mission! To the sea I will get me 'Gainst hostile warriors as warden to stand.
pairs: It is time for me to go;
may the Father who rules all
I will go back to the sea,
lines.source: Beowulf 316-319, the coast watchman's parting
lines.who_would_say_it: an English reeve, watchman or pilot who has seen the player safely in
lines.when_it_fits: a guide or watchman leaves the player at the edge of his ground

lines.original: ūre ǣghwylc sceal ende gebīdan worolde līfes; wyrce sē þe mōte dōmes ǣr dēaðe!
lines.english: Each of us must the end-day abide of His earthly existence; who is able accomplish Glory ere death!
lines.source: Beowulf 1386-1388
lines.who_would_say_it: an English lord; the player's oldest crewman
lines.when_it_fits: the old age of the player; the choice between a safe trade and a remembered one

lines.original: sēlre bið ǣghwǣm, þæt hē his frēond wrece, þonne hē fela murne;
lines.english: for each it is better, His friend to avenge than with vehemence wail him;
pairs: It is better for any man
lines.source: Beowulf 1384-1385
lines.who_would_say_it: a kinsman of someone killed; a crewman after a raid
lines.when_it_fits: a feud is offered to the player: take up the killing or take the wergild

lines.original: feor-cȳððe bēoð sēlran gesōhte þǣm þe him selfa dēah.
lines.english: Faraway countries he were better to seek for Who trusts in himself.
pairs: by a man who is himself worth something.
lines.source: Beowulf 1838-1839
lines.who_would_say_it: an English lord sending the player abroad with his goods or his son
lines.when_it_fits: a commission to a far port; the first crossing to a new people

lines.original: Dēað bið sēlla eorla gehwylcum þonne edwīt-līf!
lines.english: Death is more pleasant To every earlman than infamous life is!
lines.source: Beowulf 2890-2891
lines.who_would_say_it: a man the player has left in the lurch; a thane to a coward
lines.when_it_fits: the player has broken Troth and is told so to his face

lines.original: Oft him ānhaga āre gebīdeð, Metudes miltse, þēah þe he mōdcearig geond lagulāde longe sceolde hrēran mid hǫndum hrīmcealde sǣ, wadan wræclāstas: wyrd bið ful ārǣd!
lines.english: Still the lone one and desolate waits for his Maker's ruth — God's good mercy, albeit so long it tarry, in sooth. Careworn and sad of heart, on the watery ways must he Plow with the hand-grasped oar — how long? — the rime-cold sea. Tread thy paths of exile, O Fate, who art cruelty.
lines.english_by: Emily H. Hickey (d. 1924), The Academy (1881), in Cook and Tinker, Select Translations from Old English Poetry (1902)
pairs: and walk the paths of exile:
lines.source: The Wanderer 1-5 (Exeter Book, c. 975), in the spelling of Bright's Reader as in the chest
lines.who_would_say_it: an English exile, a lordless man, a crewman who has lost his house
lines.when_it_fits: a winter crossing alone; the player after the loss of a lord or a kindred

lines.original: Hwǣr cwōm mearg? hwǣr cwōm mago? hwǣr cwōm māþþumgyfa? hwǣr cwōm symbla gesetu? hwǣr sindon sęledrēamas?
lines.english: Where is the horse and the rider? Where is the giver of gold? Where be the seats at the banquet? Where be the hall-joys of old?
lines.english_by: Emily H. Hickey (d. 1924), in Cook and Tinker (1902); the scan in the chest has broken punctuation, mended here
pairs: Hwǣr cwōm mearg? hwǣr cwōm mago?
Where is the horse and the rider?
Where is the giver of gold?
Where be the seats at the banquet?
Where be the hall-joys of old?
lines.source: The Wanderer 92-93
lines.who_would_say_it: an old Englishman among ruins; a monk of a burned minster
lines.when_it_fits: the player comes back to a port that has been burned (Lindisfarne after 793, Dorestad after 834)

lines.original: hēr bið feoh lǣne, hēr bið frēond lǣne, hēr bið mǫn lǣne, hēr bið mǣg lǣne;
lines.english: Here is the passing of riches, here friends are passing away; And men and kinsfolk pass
lines.english_by: Emily H. Hickey (d. 1924), in Cook and Tinker (1902); her line goes on: 'and nothing and none may stay'
pairs: Here is the passing of riches,
hēr bið mǫn lǣne, hēr bið mǣg lǣne;
lines.source: The Wanderer 108-109 (lǣne is 'on loan')
lines.who_would_say_it: an English priest at a grave; the narrator on the last day
lines.when_it_fits: the death of a friend or kinsman; the last day's reckoning

lines.original: Mæg ic be me sylfum soðgied wrecan, siþas secgan,
lines.english: I can sing of myself a true song, of my voyages telling,
lines.english_by: Lola La Motte Iddings (death year not found: see the chest's note), in Cook and Tinker (1902)
lines.source: The Seafarer 1-2 (Exeter Book). Old English: the Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records text, sacred-texts.com/neu/ascp/a03_09.htm (the chest has only the English)
lines.who_would_say_it: an old English seaman asked for his story
lines.when_it_fits: the first day of a life (the old man's telling); a crewman's tale on a long leg

lines.original: Nap nihtscua, norþan sniwde, hrim hrusan bond, hægl feol on eorþan, corna caldast.
lines.english: The shadows of night became darker, it snowed from the north; The world was enchained by the frost; hail fell upon earth; 'Twas the coldest of grain.
lines.english_by: Lola La Motte Iddings (death year not found), in Cook and Tinker (1902)
pairs: The shadows of night became darker,
The world was enchained by the frost;
lines.source: The Seafarer 31-33. Old English: sacred-texts.com/neu/ascp/a03_09.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: an English crewman on a winter sea
lines.when_it_fits: the first snow at sea; a winter leg

lines.original: Forþon cnyssað nu heortan geþohtas, þæt ic hean streamas, sealtyþa gelac sylf cunnige;
lines.english: Yet the thoughts of my heart now are throbbing To test the high streams, the salt waves in tumultuous play.
lines.english_by: Lola La Motte Iddings (death year not found), in Cook and Tinker (1902)
pairs: Yet the thoughts of my heart now are throbbing
þæt ic hean streamas, sealtyþa gelac sylf cunnige;
To test the high streams, the salt waves in tumultuous play.
lines.source: The Seafarer 33-35. Old English: sacred-texts.com/neu/ascp/a03_09.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: an English seaman who could stay ashore and will not
lines.when_it_fits: spring, the first sailing after winter; a crewman signs on again

lines.original: leof wilcuma Frysan wife, þonne flota stondeð; biþ his ceol cumen ond hyre ceorl to ham, agen ætgeofa, ond heo hine in laðaþ, wæsceð his warig hrægl ond him syleþ wæde niwe,
lines.english: Dear is the welcome guest to the Frisian wife, when the vessel stands, his ship is come, and her husband to home, her own provider, and she calls him in, washes his weedy garment, and to him gives new raiment
pairs: and to him gives new raiment
lines.source: Maxims I 94-98 (Exeter Book). Old English: sacred-texts.com/neu/ascp/a03_13.htm; Thorpe's English as recorded in Design/content/lore/texts_more.json
lines.who_would_say_it: an English singer; any Englishman who knows Frisians
lines.when_it_fits: THE HOMECOMING: the player, a Frisian, ties up at Dorestad after a long voyage. The one period verse about a Frisian trader's house

lines.original: Scip sceal genægled, scyld gebunden,
lines.english: A ship must be nailed, a shield bound.
lines.english_by: the game's own (Thorpe's 1842 English not checked)
lines.source: Maxims I 93. Old English: sacred-texts.com/neu/ascp/a03_13.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: an English shipwright
lines.when_it_fits: a repair; a new ship laid down

lines.original: Lida biþ longe on siþe; a mon sceal seþeah leofes wenan,
lines.english: A seafarer is long on his voyage; yet a man must always look for the one he loves.
lines.english_by: the game's own (Thorpe's 1842 English not checked)
pairs: A seafarer is long on his voyage;
look for the one he loves.
lines.source: Maxims I 103. Old English: sacred-texts.com/neu/ascp/a03_13.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: the one who waits at home; a letter read aloud
lines.when_it_fits: word from home reaches the player far away; a bond strained by absence

lines.original: Mæst sceal on ceole, segelgyrd seomian.
lines.english: The mast belongs on the ship, the sailyard hanging there.
pairs: The mast belongs on the ship,
lines.source: Maxims II 24-25 (Cotton Tiberius B.i, 11th century). Old English: sacred-texts.com/neu/ascp/a15.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: an English shipman
lines.when_it_fits: stepping the mast in spring; a dismasting

lines.original: Ea of dune sceal flodgræg feran.
lines.english: A river must run downhill, flood-grey, on its way.
lines.source: Maxims II 30-31. Old English: sacred-texts.com/neu/ascp/a15.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: an English boatman or towpath man
lines.when_it_fits: the first river leg; a river in spate

lines.original: Treow sceal on eorle, wisdom on were.
lines.english: Good faith belongs in a lord, wisdom in a man.
pairs: Good faith belongs in a lord,
lines.source: Maxims II 32-33. Old English: sacred-texts.com/neu/ascp/a15.htm
lines.who_would_say_it: an English lord or reeve taking an oath
lines.when_it_fits: a Troth test; an oath sworn before witnesses

lines.original: Forsachistu diobolae? ec forsacho diabolae. end allum diobolgelde? end ec forsacho allum diobolgeldae. end allum dioboles uuercum? end ec forsacho allum dioboles uuercum and uuordum, Thunaer ende Uoden ende Saxnote ende allum them unholdum, the hira genotas sint. gelobistu in got alamehtigan fadaer? ec gelobo in got alamehtigan fadaer. gelobistu in crist godes suno? ec gelobo in crist gotes suno. gelobistu in halogan gast? ec gelobo in halogan gast.
lines.english: Do you forsake the devil? I forsake the devil. And all offerings to devils? And I forsake all offerings to devils. And all the works of the devil? And I forsake all the works and words of the devil, Thunaer and Woden and Saxnot and all the fiends that are their companions. Do you believe in God the almighty Father? I believe in God the almighty Father. Do you believe in Christ, the son of God? I believe in Christ, the son of God. Do you believe in the Holy Ghost? I believe in the Holy Ghost.

lines.original: In Godes minna ind in thes christianes folches ind unser bedhero gealtnissi, fon thesemo dage frammordes, so fram so mir Got geuuizci indi madh furgibit, so hald ih tesan minan bruodher, soso man mit rehtu sinan bruodher scal, in thiu, thaz er mig sosoma duo; indi mit Ludheren in nohheiniu thing ne gegango, zhe minan uuillon imo ce scadhen uuerhen.

Brooth unseraz emezzīgaz gib uns hiutu. endi farlāz uns sculdhi unsero, sama sō uuir farlāzzēm scolōm unserēm. endi ni gileidi unsih in costunga. auh arlōsi unsih fona ubile.
lines.english: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil.

endi ni gileidi unsih in costunga.

lines.original: Pro Deo amur et pro christian poblo et nostro commun saluament, d'ist di en auant, in quant Deus sauir et podir me dunat, si saluarai eo cist meon fradre Karlo, et in adiudha et in cadhuna cosa, si cum om per dreit son fradra saluar dist, in o quid il mi altresi fazet.
